result.summary: Pausanias describes the Rheti channels and the old border between Eleusis and Athens, with the early kings and heroes of Eleusis and the war that ended in Eleusinian submission. He then notes the sites of Eleusis, refuses to describe the Mysteries, and ends at Eleutheræ on the Bœotian border.

scenes.title: Rheti, Crocon and Eumolpus
scenes.summary: The sacred Rheti channels marked the old border. Pausanias recounts Crocon, Eumolpus, the war with Athens and the daughters of Celeus.
scenes.stakes: Erechtheus and Immaradus die in the war; Eleusis risks its independence and keeps only its Mysteries.

scenes.title: Heroes and sights of Eleusis
scenes.summary: Pausanias lists hero-chapels, Erineus, Theseus's killing of Procrustes and the Eleusinian temples. He declines to describe the sacred precinct.
scenes.stakes: Pausanias is forbidden by a dream to reveal the Mysteries.

scenes.title: Eleutheræ and the border
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the Attic border at Eleutheræ, its temple of Dionysus and the grotto where Antiope left her twins.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias refuses to reveal the Eleusinian Mysteries, citing a dream.
Candid remark that ancient pedigrees of heroes were often invented.

analysis.text: The passage ties borders and genealogies to local tradition, showing how Eleusis was absorbed into Athens yet kept its religious autonomy.
Secrecy about the Eleusinian Mysteries was strictly observed, and Pausanias's reticence reflects the religious norms of the second century AD.

legacy.text: The Eleusinian Mysteries described here remained among the most famous rites of antiquity, and their secrecy gave rise to the word mystery in later languages.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias writes in the second century AD, and he often notes when local genealogies seem invented, as he does here for Eleusis.

language_notes.text: Rheti means 'streams' or 'flowing channels' in Greek; these were salt-water inlets near Eleusis, not true rivers.
The Euripus is the narrow strait between Euboea and the mainland, famous for its changing currents; Chalcis stands on its Euboean shore.
Proserpine is the Roman name for Persephone, who with her mother Demeter was honoured in the Eleusinian Mysteries.
Poseidon is the sea god; Boreas is the North Wind, who carried off Orithyia, an Athenian princess.
Homer mentions Eumolpus only indirectly, so Pausanias notes he gives no ancestry for him.
Pamphus was an early Athenian poet of hymns; Pausanias pairs him with Homer as authority for the names of Celeus' daughters.
Heralds here means the hereditary Eleusinian family of Kerykes, who claimed descent from Ceryx.
Pluto's abduction of Proserpine (the Greek Hades and Persephone) is the myth behind the Eleusinian cult; Erineus is a traditional entry point to the underworld.
Procrustes made guests fit his bed by stretching them or cutting off their limbs; Theseus gave him the same treatment.
The Rharian plain was associated with Demeter's first sowing of grain; its barley made sacrificial cakes.
Pausanias says a dream forbids him to describe the inner sanctuary; the uninitiated were barred from seeing or hearing the mysteries.
Antiope's twins are Amphion and Zethus, who later built the walls of Thebes; she exposed them after bearing them to Zeus.

context_notes.text: Eleusis was once an independent city before being absorbed by Athens, which explains why a boundary lay here.
The Eleusinian Mysteries were secret rites of Demeter and Proserpine; Eleusis kept control of them even after joining Athens.
Hermes was the messenger god, so a son of his fittingly founded the line of heralds.
Hippothoon gave his name to one of the Attic tribes, the Hippothoontis.
Triptolemus was the Eleusinian hero who, in myth, spread Demeter's gift of grain to humankind.
Cithæron is the mountain range dividing Attica from Bœotia, where Thebes lay.

literary_notes.text: The channels are compared to rivers, but the comparison is limited to their flow, undercut by their salt water.
Pausanias speaks as a traveller, stating what he personally could not find and what others show, which marks his reliability.
The first-person 'my own idea' shows the author as an independent investigator who offers his own explanations of names.
Pausanias speaks as a skeptical critic, dismissing genealogies as invented and showing his rationalizing, evidence-minded approach to myth.
